summary: Defines RTP payload formats for Forward Error Correction packets produced by non-interleaved and interleaved parity codes. Repair packets are generated from source packets of one or more RTP streams and sent in a redundancy stream. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Sending extra repair packets with video or audio calls so lost pieces can be rebuilt.

questions: how does rtp forward error correction work
what is the flexfec repair window
subtitle: Extra XOR repair packets, sent in their own RTP stream, let a receiver rebuild lost audio, video or data packets.

tldr.problem: Real-time media sent over RTP loses packets, and earlier FEC formats for RTP had scalability issues.
tldr.mechanism: The sender XORs groups of source packets (by rows, by columns, or by an arbitrary bitmask) into repair packets and sends them in a separate redundancy RTP stream. The receiver XORs the survivors with the repair packet to rebuild a missing packet.
tldr.outcome: Source packets are left untouched, so receivers without FEC support still work by ignoring the repair stream. The formats are not backward compatible with the earlier specifications.

today: RFC 8627 is a Proposed Standard from July 2019. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Flexible FEC
sections.content:
RFC 8627 defines new RTP payload formats for Forward Error Correction (FEC) packets made by non-interleaved and interleaved parity codes. The codes are called Flexible FEC, or "FLEX FEC". The protected media can be audio, video, text or application data.

Repair packets are generated from a set of source packets taken from one or more source RTP streams. They travel in a redundancy RTP stream, separate from the source stream or streams. Lost source packets can then be reconstructed from the source and repair packets that did arrive.

The new formats address scalability issues of earlier specifications ([RFC 2733], RFC 5109 and SMPTE 2022-1). Because of the changes they are not backward compatible with those, although endpoints that do not implement this specification can still work by ignoring the repair packets.
sections.eli5: Along with the real packets, the sender mails a few extra repair packets. If a real one is lost, the repair packets help rebuild it.

sections.title: Row, Column and 2-D Parity Protection
sections.content:
All the codes use the XOR operation. The sender picks the source packets to protect, XORs them to make repair packets, and sends both in different RTP streams. Repair packets can be sent proactively or on demand after RTCP feedback such as NACK. If every source packet arrives, the repair packets are simply discarded.

Picture the source packets as a block of L columns and D rows. Row (non-interleaved) FEC XORs every L consecutive packets and yields D repair packets. Column (interleaved) FEC XORs packets whose sequence numbers are L apart and yields L repair packets. Either way, a repair packet can fully recover one missing packet among the packets it covers.

Row FEC copes better with random loss. Column FEC copes better with bursts, provided L is large enough that L packets last at least as long as the burst. 2-D FEC uses both, which handles mixed loss patterns at the cost of more overhead, but some loss patterns still defeat it.

With equal-sized packets the RFC gives the overhead as 1/L for row FEC, 1/D for column FEC and 1/L + 1/D for 2-D FEC.
sections.eli5: Lay the packets out in a grid. A repair packet for each row, or each column, lets you fill in one hole in that line. Using both rows and columns fixes more holes.

sections.title: Source and Repair Packet Formats
sections.content:
Source packets are sent as usual and are not modified. Their existing RTP sequence numbers identify them, so no extra fields are needed. That makes this a systematic code and keeps non-FEC receivers working, which is useful in multicast.

A repair packet has an RTP header followed by a FEC header and a Repair Payload. The Repair Payload covers everything after the fixed 12-byte RTP header of each source packet, including any CSRC list and header extensions. In the repair packet's RTP header the version MUST be 2 and the marker bit is set to 0 by senders. The CSRC list names the SSRCs of the protected source streams. The repair stream gets its own randomly assigned SSRC, and its CNAME SHOULD match that of the source stream it protects.

The first two bits of the FEC header, R and F, select one of three variants. Sending R=1, F=1 is forbidden (MUST NOT send, MUST ignore). The header also carries recovery fields for the P, X, CC, M and payload type bits, a 16-bit length recovery field and a 32-bit timestamp recovery field.
sections.eli5: The repair packet has a small label that says which packets it protects and what kind of repair it is. The real packets are sent unchanged.

sections.title: The Three FEC Header Variants
sections.content:
With R=0, F=0 the header carries a flexible mask. Each protected SSRC has a 16-bit SN base (lowest sequence number, allowing for wrap around) and a bitmask of 15, 46 or 110 bits. If bit j of the mask is 1, the packet with sequence number SN base + j is protected, and the first mask bit is j=0. The k bit says whether another mask follows. This can describe arbitrary patterns, including selective protection of only the packets that need it.

With R=0, F=1 the header carries fixed L (columns) and D (rows) fields of 8 bits each, so the maximum of either is 255. L=0, D=0 is reserved: MUST NOT send, MUST ignore. L>0, D=0 means row FEC only. L>0, D=1 means row FEC with column FEC to follow, and L>0, D>1 means column FEC of every L-th packet, D times. A repair packet whose L and D exceed the repair window MUST be ignored. The RFC notes that the mask is inefficient or impossible for very large blocks, where the fixed variant is more useful.

With R=1, F=0 the packet is a retransmission of a single source packet. The sequence number replaces the length recovery field, the source SSRC is in the FEC header rather than the CSRC list, and the only work needed is to prepend a new RTP header to the source packet.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of label. One lists exactly which packets are covered, one says "every so-many packets in a grid", and one just sends a single packet again.

sections.title: Building Repair Packets and Recovering Lost Ones
sections.content:
To build a repair packet, the sender forms a bit string from each protected source packet: the first 16 bits of its RTP header, its length minus 12, its timestamp, and all octets after the fixed 12-byte header (the SSRC is skipped). Shorter packets MUST be padded with zero octets at the end to the length of the longest. The XOR of these strings goes into the FEC header fields and the Repair Payload. Because of padding and the FEC header, a repair packet is larger than the packets it protects, which may push it past the path MTU.

To recover a packet, the receiver first works out which source packets a repair packet covers, using the mask or the L and D offsets. It then XORs the surviving source packets with the repair packet to recover the RTP header (up to and including the SSRC, which is set to the missing stream's SSRC) and then the payload.

For 2-D protection the receiver runs an iterative decoding loop. It repairs what it can with the row repair packets, then with the column repair packets, and repeats while the number of recovered packets keeps growing. In the RFC's worked example, packets 1 and 11 are recovered in the first iteration and packets 2 and 10 in the second, giving full recovery. The receiver SHOULD buffer packets for at least the repair window, the time spanning a FEC block, before it declares a decoding failure.
sections.eli5: If a piece of a puzzle goes missing, the sums tell you exactly what it must look like. With a grid you may need to fix a few pieces first before the others become solvable.

sections.title: Media Types, SDP and Congestion Control
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media subtype flexfec under four types: audio, video, text and application. Each has two required parameters: rate, the RTP clock rate, which SHALL be larger than 1000 Hz, and repair-window, given in microseconds. In SDP the subtype and rate go on the a=rtpmap line and repair-window goes on the a=fmtp line. Both examples in the RFC use a repair window of 200 ms (repair-window=200000) and tie source and repair streams together with the SDP FEC grouping semantics (a=ssrc-group:FEC-FR).

In offer/answer, a receiver that cannot support the offered repair window MUST reject the offer, since the sender may change the FEC configuration packet by packet. If a peer is offered both FLEX FEC and another retransmission method, it MUST answer with only FLEX FEC. The RTP Stream Identifier SDES item SHOULD NOT be used with this format.

On congestion, FEC streams can consume a significant share of limited bandwidth. Applications MUST NOT arbitrarily increase FEC protection, since doing so may lead to congestion collapse, and stronger protection MAY be applied only after the source rate has been reduced. The RFC recommends adjusting the amount and type of FEC to the observed loss rate and burst length.
sections.eli5: The two sides agree beforehand how long the receiver will wait for repairs. Sending too many repairs can clog a small pipe, so the sender should be careful.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These packets inherit the security concerns of RTP: confidentiality, integrity and source authenticity. The RFC points to SRTP as recommended where suitable, and mentions IPsec and DTLS (with RTP over UDP) as other options.

FLEX FEC adds its own concerns. Because it can protect multiple source streams, source buffers may be created that are never used, and an attacker could use them to occupy memory. Attacks on FEC parameters such as the repair window, D or L, or on the length recovery fields (without integrity protection), can force large memory allocations at the receiver. If source data does not match the FLEX FEC source partitioning, some data may be left unprotected.
sections.eli5: A bad actor could trick the receiver into saving far too much stuff, or could read or change the packets. Encrypting the stream helps.
